title: Culture, society and production systems
needs: Explain how culture, fashion, faiths and beliefs affect design.
Explain inclusive design, with examples of inclusive features.
Describe flexible manufacturing, lean manufacturing and Just in Time.
Give advantages and disadvantages of CAD, and explain CAM.
Explain ethics, WEEE, planned obsolescence, and design for maintenance and disassembly.

doNow.a: Designing so as many people as possible can use a product, whatever their age, gender or disability.

doNow.q: What does a Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) assess?
doNow.a: A product's environmental impact at each stage of its life.

doNow.q: Why does mass production lower the cost of each product?
doNow.a: Costs are spread over many products.

clues: I make a product go out of date or wear out within a set time.
I help a manufacturer keep its sales regular.

bigPicture.question: How do people, systems and computers shape the products we buy?

chunks.label: Culture
chunks.summary: The ideas, beliefs and customs that shape what people want.

items.ask: What makes one group of people's way of life different from another's?
items.text: The ideas, beliefs, customs and social behaviours of a group, shown through ritual, art and fashion.

image.alt: Dancers in colourful traditional costumes and hats at a festival.

items.ask: Why do lots of people suddenly want the same trainers?
items.text: Tastes change fast as people buy into the latest thing, showcased on social media, blogs and the internet.

image.alt: A shop window with clothes on mannequins and price signs.

items.ask: Why might a product's colour sell well in one country but not in another?
items.text: Colours and styles can mean very different things in different cultures, so research before selling abroad.

items.ask: Why might a product that suits one community be unsuitable for another?
items.text: Designers must consider how a product fits different faiths and communities, such as modest clothing.

check.a: The ideas, beliefs, customs and social behaviours of a society or group of people.

check.q: Why should designers research colours before selling a product in another country?
check.a: Colours can mean very different things in different cultures.

chunks.label: Inclusive design
chunks.summary: Designing products and places that almost anyone can use.

items.ask: Who might struggle with a product designed for a 'typical' person?
items.text: Products are often designed for the average user, which can leave others out.

items.ask: Who should a new product be designed for?
items.text: Designing so as many people as possible can use it safely, easily and with dignity, whatever their age, gender or disability.

items.ask: How have newer materials helped people who find products hard to hold or move?
items.text: Make products lighter, tougher and more adaptable, helping people with weaker grip and reduced mobility.

image.alt: A lightweight wheelchair with a blue metal frame.

items.ask: What could you add to a building or product so disabled and elderly people can use it?
items.text: Features such as clear signage, step-free access to buildings and transport, easy-grip handles and accessible controls.

image.alt: Four inclusive features: clear signage, step-free access, easy-grip handles and accessible controls.

check.a: Designing so as many people as possible can use a product safely, easily and with dignity, whatever their age, gender or disability.

check.q: Give two features that make a product or building more inclusive.
check.a: Any two of: clear signage, step-free access, easy-grip handles, accessible controls.

chunks.label: Manufacturing methods
chunks.summary: Systems that adapt to changing orders and cut out waste.

items.ask: What would a factory need if its orders kept changing in size and type?
items.text: Production that adapts easily to changes in the quantity or type of product being made.

image.alt: A robot loading several CNC machines that make different products.

items.ask: How can the same machines switch to making something different?
items.text: Automated machines are reprogrammed or reconfigured quickly for a new product or quantity.

items.ask: How does a factory keep track of every part and every job?
items.text: Tracks every part in the warehouse, and a production plan sets times for accessing parts, machining, assembly and packing.

items.ask: How could a factory cut its costs without making less?
items.text: Minimising waste and improving efficiency, which saves cost and reduces the use of resources.

items.ask: What kinds of waste could a factory get rid of?
items.text: Removing wasted materials, time and effort is core to lean practice.

check.q: What is a flexible manufacturing system (FMS)?
check.a: Production that adapts easily to changes in the quantity or type of product being made.

check.q: What does lean manufacturing focus on?
check.a: Minimising waste and improving efficiency, which saves cost.

chunks.label: Just in Time
chunks.summary: Ordering materials only when they are needed.

items.ask: How could a factory avoid keeping piles of stock waiting around?
items.text: Materials are ordered only as needed by closely monitoring stock, so products are made to order.

image.alt: A store full of stock beside a small amount, with a delivery arriving only as needed.

items.ask: What does a factory gain by not storing lots of stock?
items.text: Saves storage space, frees factory space, stock doesn't go out of date and cash flow stays in control.

items.ask: What could go wrong if parts arrive just before they're needed?
items.text: Needs a fast, reliable supply chain; any delay hits sales, and small orders lose bulk discounts.

check.a: Ordering materials and components only as they are needed, so products are made to order.
It needs a fast, reliable supply chain, delays affect sales, or costs are higher because small orders lose bulk discounts.

chunks.label: CAD and CAM
chunks.summary: Computers used to design products and to control the machines that make them.

items.ask: How can designers draw a product precisely without pencil and paper?
items.text: Using a computer to produce precise 2D drawings or 3D models, easy to edit and visualise before manufacture.

image.alt: CAD software on screen showing a 3D model of tanks and a platform.

items.ask: Why would a designer choose a computer over drawing by hand?
items.text: Accurate, easily changed, shared at once, rendered to show the finish, and turned into 3D models.

items.ask: What are the downsides of designing on a computer?
items.text: Costly software, computers and printers; work can be lost, corrupted or hacked; it takes time to learn.

items.ask: How can a design on a screen be turned straight into a real part?
items.text: Software turns CAD data into instructions that control machines such as laser cutters, CNC mills and 3D printers.

image.alt: A 3D model of a block with tool paths drawn around its slot and holes.

items.ask: Why do factories let computers control their machines?
items.text: Increases productivity and is highly accurate and consistent, which reduces waste.

check.a: Any two of: accurate, easy to change, can be shared at once, can be rendered to show the finish, 3D models can be made.
Uses software to turn CAD data into instructions that control machines such as laser cutters and CNC mills.

chunks.label: Ethics
chunks.summary: Thinking about the harm to people and the planet, and the laws on electrical waste.

items.ask: How could a designer check a new material won't harm the environment?
items.text: Carry out a life cycle assessment (LCA) to see how the material is likely to affect the environment.

items.ask: Why are companies keen to show they care about people and the planet?
items.text: Consumers demand it, so companies build environmental and social credentials and consider their ecological footprint.

items.ask: What wrong ways could a company use to cut its production costs?
items.text: Low or underpaid labour, compromising safety, or disposing of waste illegally.

items.ask: What could the law make businesses do about old electrical goods?
items.text: UK rules that make businesses minimise electrical waste, promote reuse and recycle correctly to meet recovery targets.

image.alt: The crossed-out wheelie bin symbol for electrical waste.

items.ask: How could an electrical product be designed so less of it is wasted?
items.text: Use less material and make products more reusable and recyclable.

check.q: Give one unethical way a company might cut its production costs.
check.a: Low or underpaid labour, compromising safety, or disposing of waste illegally.

chunks.label: Evaluating new technologies
chunks.summary: Deciding how long a product should last and what happens at the end of its life.

items.ask: Why do people end up replacing some products every couple of years?
items.text: Deliberately designing a product to go out of date or wear out within a set time, to keep sales regular.

image.alt: A small electrical appliance taken apart, with its screws beside it.

items.ask: What can make an old phone or laptop stop being useful?
items.text: Software becomes incompatible, processor power is too low or parts wear out; trends and demand matter too.

items.ask: What should happen to a product when nobody wants it any more?
items.text: Planning takeback, recovery and recycling, so disposal is efficient and cuts carbon emissions and landfill.

image.alt: Old computer monitors piled in a trailer for recycling.

items.ask: What could make a product worth fixing rather than binning?
items.text: Designing so worn out or broken parts can be replaced.

image.alt: A product with its cover unscrewed, a worn part coming out and a new part going in.

items.ask: Who gains when products are repaired instead of replaced?
items.text: Saves the whole product being thrown away and creates jobs for engineers and a spare parts supply chain.

items.ask: What would make it easier to recycle a product's parts at the end of its life?
items.text: Choosing materials so the product can be taken apart at end of life and its parts recycled or reused.

image.alt: A computer case made from cardboard, with its ports showing.

items.ask: What should a designer weigh up before using a new technology?
items.text: Cost, reliability, longevity, sustainability and recyclability.

check.a: Deliberately designing a product to go out of date or wear out within a set time.

check.q: Give one benefit of design for maintenance.
check.a: The whole product isn't thrown away, or it creates jobs for engineers and a spare parts supply chain.

Ordering materials only as they are needed.

Computer aided manufacture: software controlling machines from CAD data.
Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment regulations on electrical waste.

Designing so a product can be taken apart at end of life.

apply.q: A furniture maker makes several chair designs in small numbers each week, and the quantity of each changes all the time.
reasons: Its reprogrammable machines adapt quickly to changes in the type and quantity of product
It makes products go out of date within a set time
It lets as many people as possible use the product
It lets the product be taken apart at end of life

apply.q: A bicycle maker wants to stop paying for a large warehouse full of parts.
reasons: Parts are ordered only as they are needed, saving storage space and keeping cash flow in control
Designs can be rendered to show the final finish
Products wear out to keep sales regular
It focuses on waste, not on when stock is ordered

apply.q: A kettle maker wants customers to be able to replace a worn-out switch instead of throwing the kettle away.
reasons: Worn or broken parts can be replaced, so the whole product isn't thrown away
The product is meant to wear out within a set time
Parts are delivered only when the factory needs them

oddOne.q: Which is the odd one out?

items.why: The only one used for designing rather than making or stocking.
The only one about when materials are ordered.
The only one whose core aim is getting rid of waste.
The only one that adapts quickly to changes in the type or quantity of product.

quiz.q: What is culture?
options: The ideas, beliefs, customs and social behaviours of a group
The cost of making a product
quiz.why: Culture shows itself through ritual, art and fashion.

quiz.q: Social media, blogs and the internet let new fashions get a very rapid response from customers.
quiz.why: Products can be showcased and endorsed online, so tastes change fast.

quiz.q: A colour always means the same thing in every culture.
quiz.why: Colours and styles can carry very different meanings in different cultures.

quiz.q: Why must designers think about faiths and beliefs?
options: Some products, such as clothing, must respect religious or cultural norms
Faiths decide the price of a product
quiz.why: A product must meet the needs of different faiths and communities.

quiz.q: Inclusive design aims to let as many people as possible use a product, whatever their age, gender or disability.
quiz.why: Everyone should be able to use it safely, easily and with dignity.

quiz.q: Which is an inclusive design feature?
quiz.why: Easy-grip handles help people with weaker grip.

quiz.q: How have modern materials helped inclusive design?
options: Products are lighter, tougher and more adaptable
Products are cheaper to throw away
quiz.why: This helps people with weaker grip and reduced mobility.

quiz.q: What is a flexible manufacturing system (FMS)?
options: Production that adapts easily to changes in quantity or type
quiz.why: Reprogrammable, automated machines can switch quickly.

quiz.q: In an FMS, every part in the warehouse can be traced with an item tracking system.
quiz.why: It helps manage stock and production planning.

quiz.q: What is the core aim of lean manufacturing?
options: Storing as much stock as possible
quiz.why: Cutting waste saves cost and improves efficiency.

quiz.q: Lean manufacturing increases the use of resources.
quiz.why: It reduces the use of resources by minimising waste.

quiz.q: What does JIT stand for?
quiz.why: Materials arrive just in time to be used.

quiz.q: Which is an advantage of JIT?
quiz.why: Materials are ordered as needed, so little is stored.

quiz.q: JIT depends on a fast, reliable supply chain.
quiz.why: Any delay in deliveries affects production and sales.

quiz.q: With JIT, ordering in small quantities can mean higher costs.
quiz.why: Small orders miss out on bulk discounts.

quiz.q: Which is a disadvantage of CAD?
options: Work can be lost, corrupted or hacked
quiz.why: Other disadvantages are cost and the time taken to learn the software.

quiz.q: CAD designs can be rendered to show what the final finish will look like.
quiz.why: This helps visualise the product before manufacture.

quiz.q: What does CAM do?
options: Turns CAD data into instructions that control machines
quiz.why: Software controls machines such as laser cutters and CNC mills.

quiz.q: Which of these is an unethical way to cut production costs?
quiz.why: Low or underpaid labour, unsafe practices and illegal waste disposal are unethical.

quiz.q: The WEEE regulations require UK businesses to recycle electrical waste correctly and promote reuse.
quiz.why: They must also minimise waste and meet material recovery targets.

quiz.q: What is planned obsolescence?
options: Designing a product to go out of date or wear out within a set time
Designing a product so parts can be replaced
Designing a product to be taken apart
quiz.why: It is a deliberate strategy to keep sales regular.

quiz.q: Design for maintenance can create jobs.
quiz.why: Repairs need engineers and a spare parts supply chain.

quiz.q: Design for disassembly makes products harder to recycle.
quiz.why: Products can be taken apart so parts can be recycled or reused.

quiz.q: Which is one of the key things to consider when evaluating a new technology?
quiz.why: The key considerations are cost, reliability, longevity, sustainability and recyclability.

written.q: Describe how a designer could make a kettle more inclusive for elderly users.
points: An easy-grip handle.
Lighter modern materials, so it is easier to lift with a weaker grip.
Tougher materials that are more adaptable for reduced mobility.
Accessible controls that are easy to reach and use.
Designed so it can be used safely, easily and with dignity.
written.model: The designer could give the kettle an easy-grip handle and make it from lighter modern materials, so it is easier to lift for someone with a weaker grip. Its controls could be made accessible, so elderly users can use it safely, easily and with dignity.

written.q: Explain one disadvantage to a manufacturer of using Just in Time (JIT).
points: It needs a fast, reliable supply chain (1), so any delay in deliveries stops production and affects sales (1).
Materials are ordered in small quantities (1), so the manufacturer loses bulk discounts and costs are higher (1).
written.model: JIT relies on a fast, reliable supply chain, so if a delivery is late, production stops and sales are affected.
written.note: 1 mark for the disadvantage, 1 for explaining it. One disadvantage only.

written.q: Compare design for maintenance with design for disassembly.
points: Design for maintenance lets worn or broken parts be replaced during the product's life.
Design for disassembly lets the product be taken apart at the end of its life.
Maintenance saves the whole product from being thrown away.
Disassembly lets components and materials be recycled or reused.
Maintenance creates jobs for engineers and a spare parts supply chain.
Both reduce waste and are better for the environment.
written.model: Design for maintenance lets worn or broken parts be replaced while the product is still in use, so the whole product isn't thrown away, and it creates jobs for engineers and a spare parts supply chain. Design for disassembly is about the end of the product's life: it can be taken apart so its components and materials can be recycled or reused. Both reduce waste.
written.note: Up to 2 marks for each side. Full marks need both compared.

written.q: Explain how a manufacturer could use CAD and CAM together to make a product.
points: CAD is used to produce precise 2D drawings or 3D models on a computer.
The design can be edited easily, rendered and shared before manufacture.
CAM software turns the CAD data into instructions for a machine.
Machines such as laser cutters, CNC mills or 3D printers make the parts.
CAM is highly accurate and consistent, increases productivity and reduces waste.
written.model: The product would be designed using CAD to produce precise 2D drawings or 3D models, which can be edited, rendered and shared before manufacture. CAM software then turns the CAD data into instructions that control a machine such as a laser cutter or CNC mill, making the parts accurately and consistently with less waste.

written.q: A company is deciding whether to design its new tablet computer with planned obsolescence. Evaluate this decision.
points: Customers need to replace the tablet, which keeps sales regular.
The company can bring out new versions that follow trends and customer demand.
Old tablets become obsolete as software becomes incompatible, processor power is too low or parts wear out.
More products are thrown away, adding to waste, landfill and carbon emissions.
WEEE regulations require the company to minimise electrical waste and design for reuse and recyclability.
Consumers increasingly expect companies to have environmental and social credentials.
Justified conclusion, e.g. only acceptable if the company also plans takeback and recycling, or designs for maintenance instead.
written.model: Planned obsolescence would keep the company's sales regular, because customers would need to replace their tablets as software becomes incompatible, processor power falls behind or parts wear out, and new versions could follow trends and demand. However, more tablets would be thrown away, adding to landfill and carbon emissions. The WEEE regulations require the company to minimise electrical waste and design for reuse and recyclability, and consumers increasingly expect environmental credentials. Overall it is only acceptable if the company also runs takeback and recycling, otherwise designing for maintenance would be better.

levels.text: Detailed, balanced points on both sides, with a justified conclusion.
Some points, mostly on one side, or a conclusion that isn't justified.

written.note: Tick the points made, then use the levels under the model answer to decide the mark.

written.q: Describe what the WEEE regulations require UK businesses to do.
points: Minimise waste from their electrical equipment.
Promote reuse.
Make sure waste products are recycled correctly.
Meet material recovery targets.
Design products using less material, and make them more reusable and recyclable.
written.model: UK businesses must minimise waste from their electrical equipment and promote reuse. They must make sure waste products are recycled correctly to meet material recovery targets, and design products with less material so they are more reusable and recyclable.
